topics.title: What is a Function?
topics.student_facing_name: What a function is, and how to spot one
topics.summary: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. The lecture introduces the four ways a function gets written down — a formula, a table, a graph, and a description in words — and the vertical line test, which decides whether a curve on the page is the graph of a function at all. Piecewise-defined functions are introduced here too: one function whose rule changes depending on which part of the domain the input falls in.
method_steps: Identify the input (independent variable) and the output (dependent variable)
Check the defining condition: does every allowed input give exactly one output?
For a graph, apply the vertical line test — if any vertical line meets the curve twice, it is not a function
State the domain: the set of inputs the rule actually accepts
For a piecewise function, decide which piece the input falls in before evaluating

worked_examples.problem: Is the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ the graph of a function of $x$?
worked_examples.context: the vertical line $x = 0$ meets it at $y = 1$ and $y = -1$, so one input gives two outputs. The lecture notes that the upper half alone, $y = \sqrt{1 - x^2}$, is a function.
straight substitution; this is the cost function used repeatedly later in the course

applied_contexts: the shape of the Gateway Arch as a function
the cable of a suspension bridge as a near-parabola
cost as a function of quantity produced
common_errors: Thinking two different inputs may not share an output — that is allowed; it is two outputs from one input that is forbidden
Applying a horizontal line test instead of a vertical one
Evaluating a piecewise function with the wrong piece
Confusing the range (outputs actually reached) with the codomain
topics.geogebra_prompt: Drag a point along the graph of $y = f(x)$ and watch the input arrow on the $x$-axis and the output arrow on the $y$-axis move together

topics.title: The Elementary Functions
topics.student_facing_name: The families of functions used all term
topics.summary: A tour of the function families the rest of the course is built from: linear, power, polynomial, rational, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic. The point is recognition — being able to look at a formula and know what shape to expect, and to look at a graph and name the family.
method_steps: Look at how $x$ appears: to a fixed power, in a denominator, under a root, or in an exponent
Linear: degree one, straight line, constant slope
Power: a single term $x^a$; the sign and size of $a$ set the shape
Polynomial: a finite sum of whole-number powers, defined for every $x$
Rational: one polynomial over another, undefined where the bottom is zero
Algebraic: built from these with roots as well
Exponential: $x$ in the exponent, growth or decay; logarithmic: its inverse

worked_examples.answer: Rational — a polynomial divided by a polynomial.
worked_examples.context: and since $x^2 + 5$ is never zero, this one is defined for every $x$

applied_contexts: cost and revenue as polynomials
exponential growth and decay
rational functions in purification-cost models
common_errors: Calling $x^2$ exponential — the variable is in the base, not the exponent
Forgetting that a rational function is undefined where the denominator vanishes
Treating $\sqrt{x}$ as a polynomial
topics.geogebra_prompt: Type any formula into a plotter and compare the shapes of $x$, $x^2$, $1/x$, $\sqrt{x}$ and $e^x$ on the same axes

topics.title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions
topics.student_facing_name: When a function rises and when it falls
topics.summary: A function is increasing on an interval if larger inputs always give larger outputs there, and decreasing if larger inputs always give smaller outputs. This is defined here purely from the graph and from inequalities — no calculus yet. The same words come back much later as the First Derivative Test, so the vocabulary is worth getting right now.
method_steps: Pick the interval you are describing — a function is rarely increasing everywhere
Take any two inputs $x_1 < x_2$ inside it
Compare $f(x_1)$ and $f(x_2)$
If the output always rises, it is increasing there; if it always falls, decreasing
Read this off the graph left to right: uphill is increasing, downhill is decreasing

worked_examples.problem: On which intervals is $y = x^2$ increasing, and on which decreasing?
worked_examples.context: read straight off the parabola — downhill to the left of the vertex, uphill to the right

applied_contexts: describing whether a cost is still rising
reading a growth curve
common_errors: Saying a function 'is increasing' with no interval attached
Confusing increasing with positive — a function can be negative and still increasing
Reading the graph right to left
topics.geogebra_prompt: Drag two points along a curve and watch which way the output moves as the input increases

topics.title: Even and Odd Functions
topics.student_facing_name: Symmetry: even and odd functions
topics.summary: An even function satisfies $f(-x) = f(x)$ and its graph is a mirror image across the $y$-axis — $y = x^2$ is the standard example. An odd function satisfies $f(-x) = -f(x)$ and its graph is unchanged by a half-turn about the origin — $y = x^3$ is the standard example. Most functions are neither.
method_steps: Replace every $x$ in the formula with $-x$
Simplify, being careful with signs on odd powers
If the result is identical to $f(x)$, the function is even
If the result is $-f(x)$ throughout, the function is odd
If it is neither, say so — that is the usual answer

worked_examples.answer: $y(-x) = (-x)^2 = x^2 = y(x)$, so it is even.
worked_examples.context: check numerically first: $y(-1) = 1$ and $y(1) = 1$ are the same value
numerically, $y(-1) = -1$ and $y(1) = 1$ — each is the negative of the other
$|-x| = |x|$ and $(-x)^2 = x^2$, so every term is unchanged

applied_contexts: halving the work of sketching a symmetric graph
common_errors: Writing $(-x)^2 = -x^2$ — the bracket matters
Testing one value and concluding; the identity has to hold for every $x$
Assuming every function is one or the other
topics.geogebra_prompt: Reflect a curve across the $y$-axis, then rotate it half a turn about the origin, and see which functions land back on themselves

topics.title: Sums, Differences, Products and Quotients of Functions
topics.student_facing_name: Building new functions by adding and multiplying
topics.summary: Two functions can be added, subtracted, multiplied and divided to make a new function. The arithmetic is done output by output: $(f+g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$. The domain of the result is where both original functions are defined — and, for a quotient, where the bottom one is not zero.
method_steps: Write out $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ separately
Combine them with the operation asked for, at the same input $x$
Simplify
Take the domain to be the overlap of the two domains
For a quotient, remove the points where $g(x) = 0$

worked_examples.problem: A firm has revenue $R(x) = 110x$ and cost $C(x) = 7500 + 60x$. Write the profit function and find $P(100)$.
worked_examples.context: a loss of $2,500 at 100 units — the lecture uses this to show profit can be negative below the break-even point

applied_contexts: profit as revenue minus cost
average cost as total cost divided by quantity
common_errors: Dropping the bracket in $R(x) - C(x)$ and subtracting only the first term of $C$
Forgetting to exclude zeros of the denominator from the domain of a quotient
Combining a value of $f$ at one input with a value of $g$ at a different input
topics.geogebra_prompt: Plot $f$, $h$ and $g = f + h$ together and check that the heights add at each $x$

topics.title: Composition of Functions
topics.student_facing_name: Feeding one function into another
topics.summary: Composition feeds the output of one function into the input of another: $(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$. Work from the inside out. Composition is not commutative — $f \circ g$ and $g \circ f$ are usually different functions. This topic is the one the chain rule depends on entirely, so it is worth being fluent at spotting the inside and the outside function.
method_steps: Identify which function is applied first — that is the inside function
Evaluate the inside function at $x$
Substitute that whole expression wherever the outside function has its variable
Simplify
For the domain, keep only inputs the inside function accepts whose outputs the outside function also accepts

worked_examples.context: the same pairing reappears in the chain rule lecture, which is why it is set up this way here

applied_contexts: a cost that depends on quantity, which itself depends on time
common_errors: Computing $g(f(x))$ when $f(g(x))$ was asked for
Substituting only into the first occurrence of the variable
Multiplying the two functions instead of composing them
topics.geogebra_prompt: Show a value passing through $g$ and then through $f$, with both intermediate outputs marked

topics.title: Translations, Stretches and Reflections
topics.student_facing_name: Shifting, stretching and flipping a graph
topics.summary: Small changes to a formula move its graph in predictable ways. Adding a constant outside the function shifts it vertically; adding one inside shifts it horizontally, and in the opposite direction to the sign. Multiplying outside stretches or compresses vertically; multiplying inside does the same horizontally, again the other way round. Negative multipliers reflect. Once these are known, a great many graphs can be drawn from a handful of remembered shapes.
method_steps: Identify the base function whose shape you already know
Deal with changes inside the bracket first — these act horizontally and in reverse
Then changes outside — these act vertically and in the direction you expect
Apply reflections wherever a minus sign appears
Sketch by moving a few landmark points of the base graph rather than plotting from scratch

worked_examples.problem: Describe how the graph of $y = -f(x - 2) + 3$ relates to the graph of $y = f(x)$.
worked_examples.answer: Shift right by 2, reflect across the $x$-axis, then shift up by 3.
worked_examples.context: inside first (the $-2$ moves it right, not left), then the reflection, then the vertical shift

applied_contexts: recognising a shifted parabola in a cost model
sketching quickly in an exam
common_errors: Shifting left for $f(x - 2)$ instead of right — inside changes go the opposite way
Confusing $-f(x)$ with $f(-x)$
Applying the outside change before the inside one
topics.geogebra_prompt: Put sliders on $h$, $k$ and $c$ in $y = c\,f(x + h) + k$ and watch the graph move

topics.title: Angles, Radians and the Trigonometric Functions
topics.student_facing_name: Radians and the trig functions
topics.summary: Angles in calculus are measured in radians, not degrees: a full turn is $2\pi$ radians, a half turn is $\pi$, and one radian is about $57.3^\circ$. The lecture defines $\sin$, $\cos$ and $\tan$ first from a right-angled triangle and then, for any angle at all, from a point on a circle. Every later limit and derivative involving trig functions assumes radians.
method_steps: Convert degrees to radians by multiplying by $\pi/180$; convert back by multiplying by $180/\pi$
For an acute angle in a right-angled triangle, use opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse
For any angle, place it at the centre of a circle and read the coordinates of the point where it cuts the circle
$\cos$ is the horizontal coordinate, $\sin$ the vertical, and $\tan$ their ratio
Keep the calculator in radian mode

worked_examples.context: about $1.047$ radians

applied_contexts: periodic quantities
the Sandwich Theorem limit $\lim_{\theta \to 0}\sin\theta = 0$ later in the course
common_errors: Leaving the calculator in degree mode
Using triangle definitions for angles bigger than $90^\circ$ instead of the circle definition
Writing $\sin x$ as $\sin \times x$
topics.geogebra_prompt: Move a point round a unit circle and watch $\sin$ and $\cos$ read off as the two coordinates

topics.title: Cost, Revenue, Demand and Profit Functions
topics.student_facing_name: The business functions this course keeps using
topics.summary: The economic vocabulary the course returns to again and again. The demand function $p = D(x)$ gives the price at which $x$ items sell. Revenue is quantity times price, $R(x) = x\,D(x)$. Cost $C(x)$ is whatever production costs. Profit is the difference, $P(x) = R(x) - C(x)$. Every optimisation and marginal-analysis problem later in the course is built on these four.
method_steps: Read off which quantity is which — price per unit, number of units, total cost
Build revenue as quantity times price, not price alone
If a demand function is given, substitute it into $R(x) = x\,D(x)$
Form profit as revenue minus cost, keeping the whole cost expression in brackets
Simplify, and check the units make sense

worked_examples.problem: Demand is $p(x) = -0.27x + 51$ and cost is $C(x) = 2.23x^2 + 3.5x + 85$ (in thousands of dollars). Write $R(x)$ and $P(x)$.
worked_examples.context: note the bracket around the whole cost function before subtracting

worked_examples.problem: Cost is $C(x) = 2x^2 + 3x + 5$ and demand is $p(x) = 5 - 2x$. Write the profit function.

applied_contexts: break-even analysis
profit maximisation later in the course
marginal cost and marginal revenue
common_errors: Setting revenue equal to the price rather than price times quantity
Dropping the bracket when subtracting the cost function
Mixing up $p(x)$ the price and $P(x)$ the profit — the course uses both letters
topics.geogebra_prompt: Plot $R(x)$ and $C(x)$ on the same axes and mark where they cross (break-even) and where the gap is widest (maximum profit)

topics.title: What a Limit Is, Informally
topics.student_facing_name: The idea of a limit
topics.summary: A limit answers the question: as $x$ gets close to $c$, what value does $f(x)$ get close to? Crucially, the value of $f$ at $c$ itself is irrelevant — the function need not even be defined there. The lecture motivates this with a purification cost $C(x) = \frac{8x^2 - 636x - 320}{x^2 - 68x - 960}$, which gives $\frac{0}{0}$ at $x = 80$ yet clearly heads for $7$, and with $f(x) = \frac{x^2-1}{x-1}$, which equals $x + 1$ everywhere except at $x = 1$.
method_steps: Ask what happens near $c$, not at $c$
Try substituting; if you get an ordinary number, that is usually the limit
If you get $\frac{0}{0}$, the expression can almost always be simplified first
Cancel the common factor and substitute again
State the limit as a number, and remember it may differ from $f(c)$ or exist where $f(c)$ does not

worked_examples.context: $\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1} = x + 1$ for every $x \ne 1$, so the function heads for $1 + 1 = 2$ even though $f(1)$ is $\frac{0}{0}$ and undefined

worked_examples.problem: For the purification cost $C(x) = \frac{8x^2 - 636x - 320}{x^2 - 68x - 960}$, find $\lim_{x \to 80} C(x)$.

applied_contexts: the cost of removing the last percent of a pollutant
instantaneous speed, later in the course
common_errors: Concluding the limit does not exist as soon as substitution gives $\frac{0}{0}$
Insisting the limit must equal $f(c)$
Cancelling a factor without noting the cancellation is only valid for $x \ne c$
topics.geogebra_prompt: Show a graph with a hole at $x = c$ and a point sliding toward the hole from both sides

topics.title: Limits of the Simplest Functions
topics.student_facing_name: The two limits everything else is built from
topics.summary: Before the limit laws can be used, two starting limits are needed. For the constant function $f(x) = b$, the output never changes, so $\lim_{x \to a} b = b$. For the identity function $f(x) = x$, the output is the input, so $\lim_{x \to a} x = a$. Every polynomial limit in the course is these two combined by the limit laws.
method_steps: Recognise whether the function is constant or the identity
For a constant, the limit is that same constant whatever $a$ is
For the identity, the limit is $a$ itself
Use these as the base cases when breaking a harder limit apart

worked_examples.context: the function is the constant $5$; where $x$ is going makes no difference

common_errors: Writing $\lim_{x \to 3} 5 = 3$ — substituting into the arrow rather than the function

topics.title: When a Limit Does Not Exist
topics.student_facing_name: Limits that do not exist
topics.summary: Not every limit exists. The lecture gives the three ways it can fail at a point: the function approaches different values from the left and from the right (a jump); it grows without bound; or it oscillates and never settles. In each case the answer is 'does not exist', abbreviated DNE — and that is a complete answer, not a failure to finish.
method_steps: Approach from the left and record the value the function heads for
Approach from the right and do the same
If the two differ, the two-sided limit does not exist
If the values grow without bound, the limit does not exist as a number
If the function keeps oscillating, the limit does not exist

worked_examples.context: for $x > 0$ the function equals $1$; for $x < 0$ it equals $-1$. The one-sided limits are $1$ and $-1$, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

applied_contexts: a price that jumps at a threshold quantity
common_errors: Answering $0$ because the two sides 'cancel out'
Treating $\infty$ as a number and calling that the limit
Assuming a limit must exist because the formula looks harmless
topics.geogebra_prompt: Show $x/|x|$ with the left and right branches at different heights

topics.title: The Limit Laws
topics.student_facing_name: The rules for breaking a limit apart
topics.summary: Limits distribute over the ordinary operations. The limit of a sum is the sum of the limits, and the same holds for differences, products, quotients (provided the bottom limit is not zero), constant multiples, powers and roots. This is what lets a complicated limit be broken into pieces small enough to use the two base limits on.
method_steps: Break the expression at its top-level operation
Apply the matching law to split the limit
Keep splitting until only constants and $x$ remain
Evaluate each base limit
Reassemble — and before using the quotient rule, check the denominator's limit is not zero

worked_examples.context: difference rule gives $\lim x^2 - \lim 3x = (\lim x)^2 - 3(\lim x) = 4 - 6 = -2$
the root rule moves the limit inside: $\sqrt{1 - (1-1)^2} = \sqrt{1} = 1$

common_errors: Using the quotient rule when the denominator's limit is zero
Splitting a limit that does not exist into pieces that do
Losing the constant when applying the constant multiple rule

topics.title: Limits of Polynomials and Rational Functions
topics.student_facing_name: Limits you can do by substituting
topics.summary: For a polynomial, the limit as $x \to c$ is just the value at $c$ — substitution always works. For a rational function, substitution works too, provided the denominator is not zero at $c$. This is the first thing to try on any limit; only if it produces $\frac{0}{0}$ does more work become necessary.
method_steps: Substitute $c$ into the expression
If the result is an ordinary number, that is the limit and you are done
If the denominator comes out zero but the numerator does not, the limit does not exist as a number
If both come out zero, go on to the indeterminate-form techniques

worked_examples.context: polynomial, so substitute: $1 + 3 + 1 = 5$
denominator at $-1$ is $6 \ne 0$, so substitute: numerator is $-1 + 4 - 3 = 0$, giving $\frac{0}{6} = 0$

common_errors: Doing elaborate algebra on a limit that substitution would have settled at once
Reporting $\frac{0}{6}$ as undefined — it is $0$; it is $\frac{6}{0}$ that is the problem

topics.title: Limits Giving 0/0: Factoring and Rationalizing
topics.student_facing_name: What to do when substituting gives 0/0
topics.summary: When substitution gives $\frac{0}{0}$ the expression is telling you there is a common factor to remove, not that the limit fails. Two techniques do almost all the work in this course: factor the top and bottom and cancel the offending factor, or — when a square root is involved — multiply by the conjugate to clear it. The lecture warns explicitly that these two, cancellation and rationalization, are the ones to have ready.
method_steps: Substitute first and confirm you really have $\frac{0}{0}$
If $x = c$ makes both top and bottom vanish, then $(x - c)$ is a factor of each — that is how you know what to look for
Factor and cancel $(x - c)$
If there is a square root, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate instead, and simplify
Substitute again into the simplified expression

worked_examples.context: multiply by $\frac{\sqrt{9+h}+\sqrt{9}}{\sqrt{9+h}+\sqrt{9}}$; the top becomes $h$, which cancels, leaving $\frac{1}{\sqrt{9+h}+3} \to \frac{1}{6}$

applied_contexts: every derivative computed from the definition
common_errors: Cancelling terms rather than factors
Multiplying by the conjugate on the top only and forgetting the bottom
Expanding the conjugate product instead of using the difference of two squares

topics.title: The Sandwich Theorem
topics.student_facing_name: Trapping a limit between two others
topics.summary: If a function is trapped between two others that both head for the same value, it has no choice but to head there too. The lecture's use of this is $-|\theta| \le \sin\theta \le |\theta|$: both outer functions go to $0$ as $\theta \to 0$, so $\lim_{\theta \to 0}\sin\theta = 0$. This is a result Thomas' Calculus covers but the outline does not list separately, and it comes up again when continuity of the trig functions is claimed.
method_steps: Find a function below and a function above that both bound the one you want
Check the inequality really holds near the point (it need not hold everywhere)
Take the limit of the lower bound and of the upper bound
If they agree, the trapped function has the same limit

worked_examples.context: since $-|\theta| \le \sin\theta \le |\theta|$ and both $\pm|\theta| \to 0$, the Sandwich Theorem forces $\sin\theta \to 0$

applied_contexts: proving the trig functions are continuous at $0$
common_errors: Using bounds that do not both tend to the same value
Forgetting the inequality only needs to hold near the point
topics.geogebra_prompt: Plot $y = |x|$, $y = -|x|$ and $y = \sin x$ together near the origin

topics.title: The Precise Definition of a Limit
topics.student_facing_name: The precise ($\epsilon$–$\delta$) definition
topics.summary: The informal 'gets close to' is made exact. Distance on the number line is $|x_2 - x_1|$. Saying $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ means: however small a tolerance $\epsilon > 0$ someone demands on the output, you can supply a tolerance $\delta > 0$ on the input such that $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ guarantees $|f(x) - L| < \epsilon$. The lecture works this through concretely for $f(x) = 2x$ at $x = 1$ before stating it in general. The outline gives this a full session; the lecture deck for it is short, so treat it as an idea to understand rather than a technique to drill.
method_steps: Write the output requirement as $|f(x) - L| < \epsilon$
Rewrite it in terms of $|x - c|$ using algebra
Read off how small $|x - c|$ has to be — that is your $\delta$
State $\delta$ in terms of $\epsilon$, so it works for every tolerance, not just one
Note the strict $0 < |x - c|$: the point $x = c$ itself is deliberately excluded

worked_examples.problem: For $f(x) = 2x$, how close must $x$ be to $1$ to force $|f(x) - 2| < 0.1$?
worked_examples.context: $|2x - 2| = 2|x - 1| < 0.1$ gives $|x - 1| < 0.05$. The same argument with a general $\epsilon$ gives $\delta = \epsilon/2$, which is why any tolerance at all can be met.

applied_contexts: manufacturing tolerance: how tightly must the input be controlled to keep the output within spec
common_errors: Choosing $\delta$ for one particular $\epsilon$ and stopping there
Getting the roles the wrong way round — $\epsilon$ constrains the output, $\delta$ the input
Forgetting that $x = c$ is excluded by the strict inequality $0 < |x - c|$
topics.geogebra_prompt: Show an $\epsilon$-band around $L$ on the $y$-axis and the $\delta$-interval it forces around $c$ on the $x$-axis

topics.title: One-Sided Limits
topics.student_facing_name: Approaching from the left and from the right
topics.summary: A one-sided limit restricts the approach to one direction: $\lim_{x \to c^+}f(x)$ comes in from above, $\lim_{x \to c^-}f(x)$ from below. The two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree. One-sided limits are also what makes limits meaningful at the endpoint of a domain, where approach from one side is all there is.
method_steps: Decide which side you are approaching from
Use only the part of the rule that applies on that side — for a piecewise function, the relevant piece; for $|x|$, the relevant sign
Evaluate that one-sided limit
Repeat on the other side
The two-sided limit exists only if both exist and are equal

worked_examples.problem: For $f(x) = \frac{x}{|x|}$, find both one-sided limits at $0$.
worked_examples.context: for $x > 0$, $|x| = x$ so $f(x) = 1$; for $x < 0$, $|x| = -x$ so $f(x) = -1$. They differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

worked_examples.answer: $0$ from the left; from the right it does not exist.
worked_examples.context: for $x > 10$ the expression under the root is negative, so the function is not defined there. $x = 10$ is a right endpoint of the domain, and the left-hand limit is the only one available.

applied_contexts: a cost function whose rule changes at a threshold
behaviour at the edge of a feasible range
common_errors: Using the wrong piece of a piecewise rule for the side being approached
Reading $c^-$ as 'a negative value of $c$' rather than 'from below'
Claiming the two-sided limit exists when only one side does
topics.geogebra_prompt: Drag a point toward a jump discontinuity from each side and watch the output land on two different heights

topics.title: Continuity at a Point
topics.student_facing_name: What it means for a function to be continuous
topics.summary: Informally, a continuous function is one whose graph can be drawn without lifting the pen. Precisely, $f$ is continuous at $c$ when $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ — which quietly demands three things at once: $f(c)$ exists, the limit exists, and the two are equal. At an endpoint of the domain the appropriate one-sided version is used instead.
method_steps: Check $f(c)$ is defined
Check $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ exists — both one-sided limits present and equal
Check the two numbers are the same
If all three hold, $f$ is continuous at $c$; if any fails, it is not
At an endpoint, use the one-sided limit from inside the domain

worked_examples.context: $f(0)$ is not defined, so the first condition already fails — whatever the limit does

worked_examples.problem: On what interval is $f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x^2}$ continuous?
worked_examples.context: continuous at every interior point, and one-sidedly continuous at the two endpoints $x = -2$ and $x = 2$

applied_contexts: a quantity that changes smoothly rather than jumping
common_errors: Checking the limit exists but forgetting to compare it with $f(c)$
Assuming a formula that looks tidy must be continuous everywhere
Requiring a two-sided limit at an endpoint, where only one side exists

topics.title: Removable and Non-Removable Discontinuities
topics.student_facing_name: Kinds of break in a graph
topics.summary: Discontinuities come in kinds. A removable one is a single missing or misplaced point: the limit exists, so redefining the function at that one input repairs it. A jump, where the two one-sided limits differ, and an infinite discontinuity, where the function blows up, cannot be repaired by any choice of value. The lecture's example of a repair is $f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}$, undefined at $0$ but with limit $1$ there, extended to a continuous $F$ by setting $F(0) = 1$.
method_steps: Compute both one-sided limits at the suspect point
If they agree and are finite, the discontinuity is removable — define $f$ there to equal that common value
If they are finite but different, it is a jump, and nothing can be done
If either is infinite, it is an infinite discontinuity
Say which kind it is; the classification is part of the answer

worked_examples.problem: $f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}$ is undefined at $x = 0$. Can it be made continuous there?
worked_examples.context: $\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$, so filling in the single missing point with $1$ repairs it. $f$ itself remains discontinuous at $0$; it is the extended $F$ that is continuous.
the one-sided limits are $1$ and $-1$; no single value at $0$ can bridge them

applied_contexts: a tariff that steps up at a threshold
a data series with one missing reading
common_errors: Calling a jump removable because the function is defined on both sides
Saying the original function is continuous after the repair — it is the extended function that is
Skipping the classification and only saying 'discontinuous'

topics.title: Properties of Continuous Functions and the Intermediate Value Theorem
topics.student_facing_name: What continuous functions let you do
topics.summary: Continuity survives arithmetic and composition: sums, differences, products, quotients (where the denominator is not zero) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous. So polynomials are continuous everywhere, rational functions everywhere their denominator is not zero, and $\sin$, $\cos$ and $\tan$ wherever they are defined. The Intermediate Value Theorem then says a function continuous on $[a,b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ — which is the precise version of 'the graph has no breaks'.
method_steps: Recognise the function as built from known continuous pieces
Name the construction: sum, product, quotient or composition
Exclude the points where a denominator vanishes or a root goes negative
To use the IVT, check continuity on a closed interval $[a,b]$ first
Then any value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ is attained somewhere inside

worked_examples.context: a polynomial, so built by sums and products from $x$ and constants, all of which are continuous
including at $x = 0$, where both one-sided limits are $0$ and $f(0) = 0$ — note it is continuous there even though it has a corner

applied_contexts: showing a break-even point must exist between a loss and a profit
common_errors: Using the IVT on an interval where the function is not continuous
Expecting the IVT to say where the value is reached — it says only that it is
Assuming a corner means a break; $|x|$ is continuous at $0$

topics.title: Limits at Infinity
topics.student_facing_name: What happens as $x$ gets very large
topics.summary: Here $x$ runs off to $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ and the question is what the outputs settle down to. The two facts everything rests on are $\lim_{x \to \pm\infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0$ and $\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} k = k$. For a rational function, dividing top and bottom by the highest power of $x$ turns every remaining term into something of the form $\frac{1}{x^n}$, which vanishes. A difference of the form $\infty - \infty$ has to be rearranged first, usually by the conjugate trick.
method_steps: For a rational function, find the highest power of $x$ anywhere in the expression
Divide every term, top and bottom, by that power
Send each $\frac{1}{x^n}$ to zero
Read off what is left
For an $\infty - \infty$ form involving a root, multiply by the conjugate over itself first

worked_examples.context: this is $\infty - \infty$, so multiply by $\frac{x + \sqrt{x^2+16}}{x + \sqrt{x^2+16}}$ to get $\frac{x^2 - (x^2+16)}{x + \sqrt{x^2+16}} = \frac{-16}{x + \sqrt{x^2+16}}$, whose denominator grows without bound, so the whole thing tends to $0$

applied_contexts: long-run average cost
a population approaching its carrying capacity
common_errors: Treating $\infty - \infty$ as $0$ without rearranging
Dividing by the highest power in the denominator only
Assuming a limit at $+\infty$ tells you the limit at $-\infty$
topics.geogebra_prompt: Zoom out on $y = 1/x$ and watch the curve flatten toward the $x$-axis in both directions

topics.title: Infinite Limits
topics.student_facing_name: When the function itself blows up
topics.summary: The other way round from limits at infinity: $x$ approaches an ordinary number but the outputs grow without bound. Writing $\lim_{x \to 0^+}\frac{1}{x} = +\infty$ is a description of behaviour, not a claim that the limit is a number — the limit does not exist. The sign usually depends on which side you come from, so these are almost always computed one side at a time.
method_steps: Find where the denominator is zero
Approach from one side and decide the sign of the denominator there
The numerator's sign, divided by that, gives the direction of blow-up
Repeat on the other side — the signs often differ
Report each side separately, and say the two-sided limit does not exist

worked_examples.problem: Find the one-sided limits of $\frac{1}{x+2}$ at $x = -2$.
worked_examples.context: just left of $-2$ the denominator is a small negative number; just right of it, a small positive one

applied_contexts: a cost model that becomes unbounded as a limit of purity is approached
common_errors: Writing $=\infty$ and calling the limit existent
Getting the sign wrong by not checking which side of the zero you are on
Confusing 'limit at infinity' with 'infinite limit' — they are opposite situations

topics.title: Horizontal and Vertical Asymptotes
topics.student_facing_name: Asymptotes: the lines a graph hugs
topics.summary: Asymptotes are the graphical reading of the two previous topics. A horizontal asymptote $y = b$ records that $f(x) \to b$ as $x \to +\infty$ or $-\infty$. A vertical asymptote $x = a$ records that $f(x) \to \pm\infty$ as $x \to a$ from one side or the other. Finding the asymptotes of a rational function is a matter of computing those limits.
method_steps: For horizontal asymptotes, take the limits as $x \to +\infty$ and $x \to -\infty$
Any finite value obtained gives a horizontal asymptote; the two directions can give different ones
For vertical asymptotes, find where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not
Check the one-sided limits there to confirm blow-up and record its direction
State the asymptotes as equations of lines, not as numbers

worked_examples.context: $\lim_{x \to \pm\infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0$ gives the horizontal one; $\lim_{x \to 0^+} = +\infty$ and $\lim_{x \to 0^-} = -\infty$ give the vertical one

applied_contexts: a long-run price floor
a capacity a process can never exceed
common_errors: Writing the asymptote as '$0$' rather than as the line $y = 0$
Assuming a graph can never cross a horizontal asymptote — it can
Declaring a vertical asymptote at every zero of the denominator, including ones that cancel
topics.geogebra_prompt: Plot a rational function with its asymptotes drawn as dashed lines

topics.title: Average Rate of Change and Average Speed
topics.student_facing_name: How fast something changes on average over an interval
topics.summary: The lecture opens with a car travelling at constant speed, where distance is $y = vt$ and the speed can be read off the graph as a slope. It then drops a ball from a tower, where $y = 16t^2$ feet and the speed is no longer constant, so only an *average* speed over an interval makes sense. Average rate of change is the change in the output divided by the change in the input, and geometrically it is the slope of the line joining two points on the graph.
method_steps: Identify the two endpoints of the interval
Evaluate the function at both endpoints
Divide the change in output by the change in input
If the interval is written $[x_0,\, x_0+h]$, the denominator is simply $h$
Say what the number means in the units of the problem

worked_examples.problem: A ball is dropped from a tower and falls $y = 16t^2$ feet in $t$ seconds. Find its average speed over $[1, 2]$, then over $[1, 1.1]$, $[1, 1.01]$ and $[1, 1.0001]$.
worked_examples.answer: $48$, then $33.6$, then $32.16$, then $32.0016$ feet per second.
worked_examples.context: the lecture's central table. Average speed over $[t_0, t_0+h]$ is $16\left(\dfrac{(t_0+h)^2 - t_0^2}{h}\right)$. The numbers are visibly closing in on $32$, which is the point of the exercise — it sets up the instantaneous rate in the next topic.

worked_examples.problem: A fly population is $150$ on day $22$ and $340$ on day $45$. Find the average rate of change of the population.
worked_examples.context: the professor's biology example; the units matter as much as the number

applied_contexts: average speed of a falling body
average growth rate of a population
average change in consumer expenditure per unit sold
common_errors: Subtracting the endpoints in one order in the numerator and the other order in the denominator
Dividing by the endpoint rather than by the length of the interval
Reporting a bare number with no units
Treating the average speed over an interval as the speed at one instant in it
topics.geogebra_prompt: Plot $y = 16t^2$ and a chord from $t = 1$ to a draggable second point; display the chord's slope as the point is dragged towards $t = 1$

topics.title: Average Rate versus Instantaneous Rate
topics.student_facing_name: The difference between speed over an interval and speed at an instant
topics.summary: Shrinking the interval to nothing turns an average rate into an instantaneous one. The table for the falling ball closes in on $32$ feet per second at $t = 1$, and that number is the limit of the average speeds, not any one of them. This is the whole idea of the derivative stated before the machinery arrives. The lecture ends with a historical note: Bhaskaracarya described exactly this distinction in the *Siddhanta-Siromani* (1114–1185), separating the rough motion (*sthulagati*) of a planet over a day from its fine, instantaneous motion (*tat-kalika gati*), and observing that the interval must be taken immeasurably small.
method_steps: Compute the average rate over a sequence of shrinking intervals starting at the same point
Watch what number the averages settle towards
That limiting number is the instantaneous rate at that point
Recognise this as a limit of the kind met in the limits unit, with $h \to 0$

worked_examples.problem: From the table $48,\, 33.6,\, 32.16,\, 32.0016$ for the falling ball, what is the instantaneous speed at $t = 1$?
worked_examples.context: the averages are approaching $32$ but never equal it, exactly as the values of a function approach a limit. The limit is the instantaneous speed.

worked_examples.problem: The fly population is $150$ on day $22$ and $340$ on day $45$. Is the rate of growth *at* day 23 the same as the average rate over those 23 days?
worked_examples.context: the average over the whole period smooths out the variation. The rate at day 23 is the slope of the tangent at that single point, which the professor reads off the graph rather than computing.

applied_contexts: speedometer reading versus average speed for a journey
growth rate on one day versus over a season
instantaneous motion of a planet in twelfth-century Indian astronomy
common_errors: Believing the instantaneous rate is just the average over a very short interval, rather than the limit of those averages
Trying to set $h = 0$ directly and getting $0/0$
Assuming the average rate over an interval is attained at its midpoint
topics.geogebra_prompt: A slider for $h$ on the graph of $y = 16t^2$: as $h \to 0$ the secant through $(1, 16)$ and $(1+h, 16(1+h)^2)$ rotates into the tangent

topics.title: The Derivative: Secant and Tangent Lines
topics.student_facing_name: Understanding instantaneous rate of change via secants and tangents
topics.summary: The derivative as the slope of the tangent line, reached as the limit of the slopes of secant lines. The lecture starts with the tangent to a circle — a line meeting it once — then warns that for a general curve the useful definition is not 'meets the curve once' but 'the limiting position of the secants'. With $P = (a, f(a))$ and $Q = (z, f(z))$, the secant slope is $m_{PQ} = \dfrac{f(z) - f(a)}{z - a}$; writing $z = a + h$ turns this into $\dfrac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$, and letting $Q \to P$ gives the slope of the tangent.
notation: instantaneous rate of change $=$ slope of the tangent
method_steps: Mark the fixed point $P = (a, f(a))$ and a nearby point $Q = (z, f(z))$ on the curve
Write the secant slope $m_{PQ} = \dfrac{f(z) - f(a)}{z - a}$
Substitute $z = a + h$ so the slope becomes $\dfrac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$
Let $Q \to P$, that is $h \to 0$
The limit of the secant slopes is the slope of the tangent at $P$, written $f'(a)$
applied_contexts: marginal cost (instantaneous rate of change of cost)
marginal revenue (instantaneous rate of change of revenue)
velocity (instantaneous rate of change of position)
rate of growth (population, bacteria, etc.)
common_errors: Confusing average rate of change with instantaneous rate of change
Defining a tangent as a line meeting the curve exactly once — true for a circle, false in general
Thinking a tangent may never cross the curve
Setting $h = 0$ in the secant slope instead of taking the limit
topics.geogebra_prompt: f(x) = x^2; Create a secant through (a, f(a)) and (a+h, f(a+h)); use slider to shrink h toward 0

topics.title: The Derivative by First Principle (Limit Definition)
topics.student_facing_name: Computing derivatives from the definition
topics.summary: The derivative of $f$ at $x_0$ is the limit of the difference quotient: $f'(x_0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(x_0+h) - f(x_0)}{h}$. The professor calls the quotient $\dfrac{f(x_0+h) - f(x_0)}{h}$ (with $h \ne 0$) the difference quotient, and states the definition as 'the derivative of $f$ at $x_0$ is equal to the limit of the difference quotient of $f$'. Everything else in the course is built on this, and the rules that come later are shortcuts for it.
method_steps: Write $f(a+h)$ by substituting $(a+h)$ into the function
Compute $f(a+h) - f(a)$ and simplify
Form the quotient $\frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$
Simplify (usually by canceling $h$ or rationalizing)
Take the limit as $h \to 0$

worked_examples.problem: For $f(x) = \frac{x^2}{3} + 5x$, compute the instantaneous rate of change at $x = 2$ using the first principle.
worked_examples.context: students should show all steps: $f(2+h) = \frac{(2+h)^2}{3} + 5(2+h)$, expand, simplify difference quotient, cancel $h$, take limit

worked_examples.problem: For $f(x) = x^2 + 10x$, compute the slope of the tangent line at $x = 2$ using the first principle.
worked_examples.context: polynomial expansion and cancellation

worked_examples.problem: Find the slope of the curve $f(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}$ at the point $x = 8$ using the first principle.
worked_examples.answer: $f'(8) = \frac{1}{6}$. Steps: $f(8+h) = \sqrt{9 + h}$. $f(8+h) - f(8) = \sqrt{9+h} - 3$. Rationalize: $\frac{\sqrt{9+h} - 3}{h} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{9+h} + 3}{\sqrt{9+h} + 3} = \frac{9 + h - 9}{h(\sqrt{9+h} + 3)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{9+h} + 3}$. As $h \to 0$, this approaches $\frac{1}{6}$.
worked_examples.context: rationalization of square root expressions

worked_examples.problem: Use the limit definition (first principle) of the derivative to find the derivative of $f(x) = 3x^2 + 8$ at $x = 4$.
worked_examples.context: standard polynomial derivative from first principles

worked_examples.problem: Use the limit definition (first principle) of the derivative to find the derivative of $f(x) = \frac{5}{2 + 5x}$ at $x = 10$.
worked_examples.context: rational function requiring common denominator manipulation

worked_examples.problem: Use the limit definition (first principle) of the derivative to find the derivative of $f(x) = 4x + 5$ at $x = 5$.
worked_examples.context: linear function; derivative is the slope of the line

worked_examples.problem: Use the limit definition (first principle) of the derivative to find the derivative of $f(x) = 5 - 7x^2$ at $x = 8$.
worked_examples.context: quadratic with leading negative coefficient

worked_examples.problem: Use the limit definition (first principle) of the derivative to find the derivative of $f(x) = \sqrt{35 - x}$ at $x = 10$.
worked_examples.context: square root under subtraction; requires careful rationalization

worked_examples.problem: Use the limit definition (first principle) of the derivative to find the derivative of $f(x) = \frac{3+x}{2-x}$ at $x = 8$.
worked_examples.context: rational function with both $x$ in numerator and denominator

applied_contexts: marginal cost, revenue, profit (business)
velocity, acceleration (physics)
rate of population change (biology)
common_errors: Failing to fully expand $(a+h)^2$ or $(a+h)^3$ correctly
Forgetting to divide the entire numerator by $h$, not just part of it
Not rationalizing square roots; leaving $\sqrt{a+h} - \sqrt{a}$ in the quotient
Not canceling $h$ before taking the limit
Arithmetic errors in simplifying the difference $f(a+h) - f(a)$
topics.geogebra_prompt: f(x) = x^2 + 10*x; Secant line with draggable h parameter; watch slope approach tangent as h -> 0

topics.title: The Derivative as a Function
topics.student_facing_name: Turning the derivative at a point into a function in its own right
topics.summary: Instead of fixing $x_0$ and getting a number, let the point vary and get a function. The lecture works $f(x) = 1/x$ at a general point $a$, obtaining $f'(a) = -1/a^2$, and then observes that since this holds for every $a$, the rule $f'(x) = -1/x^2$ is itself a function — the derivative function. Producing it is called differentiation. Several notations for the same object are introduced, and the graph of $f'$ is read off the graph of $f$ by reading slopes. The section closes with the fact that a differentiable function is continuous.
method_steps: Run the first-principles calculation with a general point $a$ rather than a number
Simplify the difference quotient and take the limit as $h \to 0$
Read the answer as a rule in $a$, then rename $a$ as $x$
To get the derivative at a particular point, substitute into this rule
To sketch $f'$, read the slope of $f$ at each $x$ and plot it as a height

worked_examples.problem: Differentiate $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ from first principles at a general point $a$.
worked_examples.context: $\dfrac{\frac{1}{a+h} - \frac{1}{a}}{h} = \dfrac{a - (a+h)}{(a+h)a} \cdot \dfrac{1}{h} = \dfrac{-h}{(a+h)a} \cdot \dfrac{1}{h} = \dfrac{-1}{(a+h)a}$, and as $h \to 0$ this is $-1/a^2$. The professor's worked case, done slowly.

worked_examples.problem: Using $f'(x) = -1/x^2$, find the slope of $y = 1/x$ at $x = 1$.
worked_examples.context: the same answer the earlier lecture got by running first principles at $x=1$ directly — the point of having the derivative function is that this is now a substitution

applied_contexts: velocity as a function of time, from position as a function of time
marginal cost as a function of quantity, from total cost
reading the shape of a graph from the sign of its derivative
common_errors: Treating $f'(x)$ and $f'(a)$ as the same object — one is a function, the other a number
Reading $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ as a fraction of two quantities that can be separated
Writing $\dfrac{d}{dx}$ with nothing after it to differentiate
Sketching $f'$ by copying the shape of $f$ instead of plotting its slopes
topics.geogebra_prompt: Show $f(x)$ with a moving tangent and, underneath, a point tracing $(x, f'(x))$ so the derivative graph is drawn out as the tangent slides

topics.title: Functions with No Derivative at a Point
topics.student_facing_name: Where a curve has no tangent, and why
topics.summary: A function can fail to be differentiable at a point even where it is perfectly well defined. The lecture lists the ways: a corner, where the slope from the left and the slope from the right disagree; a cusp; a vertical tangent, as $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ has at $x = 0$; and any discontinuity. The last of these follows from the theorem stated at the end of the section — if $f$ is differentiable at a point it is continuous there — read the other way round: a break in the graph rules out a derivative.
method_steps: Check first whether the function is continuous at the point; if not, there is no derivative
Compute the difference quotient's limit from the left and from the right separately
If the two one-sided limits differ, the graph has a corner and there is no derivative
If both are infinite in the same direction, the tangent is vertical and there is no derivative
Only if the two agree and are finite does the derivative exist

worked_examples.answer: No — the tangent there is vertical.
worked_examples.context: the difference quotient $\dfrac{\sqrt{h}}{h} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{h}} \to +\infty$ as $h \to 0^{+}$. The curve is continuous at $0$ but has no slope there.
from the right the difference quotient is $h/h = 1$; from the left it is $-h/h = -1$. Two different one-sided answers, so the limit does not exist.

applied_contexts: a tariff that changes rate at a threshold, giving a kink in the cost curve
an object that bounces, so velocity reverses instantaneously
common_errors: Assuming continuity is enough for differentiability — the implication runs one way only
Reporting a derivative at a corner by using only one side
Thinking a vertical tangent means the derivative is 'infinity' rather than that it does not exist
Forgetting to check the point is in the domain at all
topics.geogebra_prompt: Plot $y = |x|$ and $y = \sqrt{x}$ side by side with a tangent that follows the cursor, so it visibly jumps at the corner and rears up at the vertical tangent

topics.title: Basic Derivative Rules: Power, Constant, Exponential, Logarithm
topics.student_facing_name: Quick rules for finding derivatives
topics.summary: The shortcut rules, which replace first principles for almost every function met in this course: the derivative of a constant is zero, the power rule $\dfrac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1}$ for any real $n$, the exponential rules and the logarithm rule. The professor's own examples push the power rule past whole numbers deliberately — $x^{\sqrt{3}+1}$ appears on the board — to make the point that $n$ need not be an integer. The trigonometric derivatives are noted at the end of the lecture. A constant multiple passes straight through: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[k\,f(x)] = k\,f'(x)$.
method_steps: Identify which rule(s) apply to the function
Apply the rule(s) to each term
Simplify the result

worked_examples.context: the professor's first rules example. $\sqrt{2}$ is a constant multiplier, not something to differentiate.
chosen to show the power rule holds for irrational exponents; subtracting one from $\sqrt{3}+1$ leaves $\sqrt{3}$
the plain case, used on the slide to set the pattern before the harder ones

applied_contexts: quickly computing marginal quantities
optimizing production or revenue
common_errors: Forgetting the exponent decrease in the power rule
Confusing $\frac{d}{dx}[a^x]$ with $\frac{d}{dx}[x^a]$
Forgetting $\ln a$ in the exponential rule
Misapplying the power rule to negative or fractional exponents
topics.geogebra_prompt: y = x^3; Derivative should be 3*x^2

topics.title: Sum, Product, and Quotient Rules
topics.student_facing_name: Derivatives of sums, products, and quotients of functions
topics.summary: Sums and differences differentiate term by term. Products and quotients do not — the professor flags these as 'two more rules which are very important' precisely because students expect them to. The product rule is $\dfrac{d}{dx}[uv] = u\dfrac{dv}{dx} + v\dfrac{du}{dx}$ and the quotient rule is $\dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left[\dfrac{u}{v}\right] = \dfrac{v\frac{du}{dx} - u\frac{dv}{dx}}{v^{2}}$.
method_steps: For sum/difference: differentiate each term and add/subtract
For product: use $u \frac{dv}{dx} + v \frac{du}{dx}$
For quotient: use $\frac{v du - u dv}{v^2}$ or the mnemonic 'low d-high minus high d-low, square the bottom'
Simplify

worked_examples.context: sum rule applied term-by-term
power rule on each term
This example is also solvable by expanding or by chain rule (later)
chain rule perspective; can also expand and differentiate

worked_examples.answer: Students should note $(x^2 - 25) = (x-5)(x+5)$, so the function simplifies to $(x+5)(7x^4 + 2x^2 + 10)$ for $x \ne 5$. Then apply product rule.
worked_examples.context: simplify before differentiating

worked_examples.answer: Note $x^3 - 64 = (x-4)(x^2+4x+16)$, so $y = x^2(x^2 + 4x + 16)$ for $x \ne 4$. Then expand and differentiate.
worked_examples.context: cancellation simplifies the problem

applied_contexts: marginal profit, cost, revenue for complex functions
elasticity calculations
common_errors: Applying the product rule when sum rule is appropriate (forgetting linearity)
Reversing the order in the quotient rule numerator (u dv - v du vs. v du - u dv)
Forgetting to square the denominator in quotient rule
Not simplifying or factoring before applying the rule, leading to messy algebra
topics.geogebra_prompt: y = (x^2 - 2)^2; Compute derivative symbolically

topics.title: Differentiation of Complex Functions
topics.student_facing_name: Combining multiple rules to differentiate complicated expressions
topics.summary: Longer problems where more than one rule is needed and the algebra is the real work. The professor's classroom examples are a product of two multi-term expressions and a quotient of two surd expressions evaluated at a point. The habit being taught is to name $u$ and $v$ explicitly, differentiate each separately, then assemble — rather than trying to do the whole thing in one line.
method_steps: Identify the dominant structure (sum, product, quotient, or composition)
Apply the appropriate rule(s) and note each sub-rule used
Simplify at each step if possible

worked_examples.context: the professor's product-rule example. Set $u = \sqrt{x} + x^2 + 3$ and $v = x^3 + x - \tfrac14$; note $\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}$ before differentiating.

worked_examples.problem: For $g(s) = \dfrac{\sqrt{s} + 1}{2\sqrt{s} - 1}$, find $g'(s)$ and evaluate it at $s = 3$.
worked_examples.context: the professor's quotient-rule example, with the variable called $s$ rather than $x$ on purpose. The numerator simplifies a long way before substituting.

applied_contexts: complex economic models
optimization in multi-factor systems
common_errors: Losing track of which rule to apply in multi-layered expressions
Arithmetic errors in combining terms
Not fully simplifying the final answer
Applying rules in the wrong order
topics.geogebra_prompt: y = (5-ln(x))/x^5; Compute and plot derivative

topics.title: Second and Higher-Order Derivatives
topics.student_facing_name: Taking derivatives of derivatives
topics.summary: Differentiating twice. The professor writes it as $\left(f'\right)' = f''$ and reads $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$ as the derivative of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. Higher orders follow the same pattern. The second derivative is a rate of change of a rate of change — acceleration is the standard example — and it is the tool the second derivative test uses later to tell a maximum from a minimum.
method_steps: Find the first derivative $f'(x)$
Differentiate $f'(x)$ to obtain $f''(x)$
Repeat if higher orders are required

worked_examples.context: the slide's own example; the second derivative is just the rule applied again

worked_examples.problem: A particle falls with $x(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^{2}$. Find its velocity and its acceleration.
worked_examples.context: the professor's physics case: the acceleration is constant, which is what makes free fall the standard example

common_errors: Forgetting to apply the power rule completely when taking second derivatives
Confusing notation: $f''$ means derivative of $f'$, not squaring $f$
topics.geogebra_prompt: Plot y = x^3 - 3x^2 + 1, then plot its first derivative, then its second derivative to see how concavity changes

topics.title: Chain Rule
topics.student_facing_name: Derivatives of composite functions
topics.summary: For a composition, the derivatives multiply. If $y = f(u)$ and $u = g(x)$ then $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{du}\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx}$, equivalently $\dfrac{d}{dx}f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))\,g'(x)$. The professor states it both ways on consecutive slides, because the Leibniz form is easier to remember and the prime form is easier to apply. Nested compositions are handled by working from the outside in, one layer at a time.
method_steps: Identify the outer function and inner function
Differentiate the outer function with respect to the inner function
Multiply by the derivative of the inner function
Simplify

worked_examples.context: the professor's hardest chain-rule example — three layers. Peel from the outside: outer square root, then $1 - \sqrt{1-x}$, then $1-x$. The two minus signs cancel, which is where students go wrong.
the professor's introductory case, stated in the $y = f(u)$, $u = g(x)$ form
a one-layer composition where the inner derivative is the constant $-2$
the inner function is a whole polynomial; differentiate it as one object
the professor's abstract version — no formula for $g$ is given, only its values, so the chain rule has to be applied symbolically

applied_contexts: growth models with exponential and logarithmic components
compound rate changes
common_errors: Forgetting to multiply by the derivative of the inner function
Misidentifying which is the outer and which is the inner function
Applying the chain rule when not needed (e.g., $(2x)^2$ is not a composition)
topics.geogebra_prompt: y = (9*x^2 - 5*x + 100)^3; Verify derivative by numerical differentiation

topics.title: Implicit Differentiation
topics.student_facing_name: Differentiating equations that are not solved for y
topics.summary: Some curves are given by an equation in $x$ and $y$ that cannot, or should not, be rearranged into $y = f(x)$. The professor's examples are the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ and a four-leaved clover, neither of which passes the vertical line test, so neither is the graph of a single function. The method is to treat $y$ as a function of $x$, differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ applying the chain rule wherever $y$ appears, then solve the result for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. The answer usually contains both $x$ and $y$, which is expected: a point on the curve is needed to get a number.
notation: $y(x)$ — the dependent variable written as a function of $x$
topics.notation_warning: This course writes the dependent variable as $y(x)$ all the way through an implicit differentiation, not as a bare $y$. So the professor writes $x^2 + (y(x))^2 = 25$ and then $2x + 2y(x)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$, and his final answers keep the $y(x)$, as in $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x}{y(x)}$. Follow that notation. It is deliberate — his slide says 'Don't forget to differentiate $y(x)$ with respect to $x$' — and it is the whole point of the method, so do not silently drop the $(x)$ and write $-x/y$.
method_steps: Rewrite the equation with the dependent variable shown as $y(x)$
Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$
Every time $y(x)$ is differentiated, the chain rule contributes a factor $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$
Collect all the terms containing $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ on one side
Factor out $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and divide to solve for it
To get a number, substitute the coordinates of a point that lies on the curve

worked_examples.problem: For $y^{3} + 1 = x$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, and its value at $(2, 1)$.
worked_examples.context: the professor's first example, worked twice across two decks. Written his way: $y(x)^3 + 1 = x$, then differentiate.
a sideways parabola — two $y$ values for most $x$, so it is not a function, yet it still has a well-defined tangent at each point

worked_examples.problem: Find the slope of the circle $x^{2} + y^{2} = 25$ at the point $(3, -4)$.
worked_examples.context: the professor's main example. Note the sign: the point has $y = -4$, and the two minus signs give a positive slope.
the $xy$ term needs the product rule as well as the chain rule — this is the example that separates students who have understood the method from those copying a pattern
product rule on the left, with the chain rule inside $e^{2x}$

applied_contexts: the slope of a circular or elliptical path at a point
curves given by an equation rather than a formula for $y$
common_errors: Differentiating a term in $y$ as though $y$ were a constant, and losing the $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ factor
Forgetting the product rule on a mixed term such as $xy$
Trying to solve the equation for $y$ first, which is often impossible and always more work
Substituting the point before differentiating rather than after
Being surprised that the answer contains $y$ — it should

topics.title: The Derivative as a Rate of Change
topics.student_facing_name: Using the derivative to model motion and cost
topics.summary: What the derivative is *for*. Two settings are developed. In motion along a line, position $s = f(t)$ has derivative $\dfrac{ds}{dt}$, the velocity, and differentiating again gives the acceleration. In economics, the derivative of a cost function $C(x)$ is the marginal cost $C'(x)$ and the derivative of a revenue function $R(x)$ is the marginal revenue $R'(x)$. The professor is careful about the two definitions of marginal cost that are in circulation: strictly it is the derivative, but it is also often defined as the cost of producing one more unit, and the two agree closely because $\dfrac{dC}{dx} \simeq \dfrac{\Delta C}{\Delta x}$ when $\Delta x = 1$ is small relative to the output.
method_steps: Identify what is changing and with respect to what
Write the relationship as a function
Differentiate to get the rate of change
Substitute the value at which the rate is wanted
State the answer with its units, and say what it means in the situation

worked_examples.problem: For $C(x) = \tfrac{1}{8}x^{2} + 3x + 98$, find the marginal cost at $x = 8$, and compare it with the actual cost of the ninth unit, $C(9) - C(8)$.
worked_examples.answer: $C'(x) = \tfrac{1}{4}x + 3$, so $C'(8) = 2 + 3 = 5$ dollars. The actual cost of the ninth unit is $C(9) - C(8) = 5.13$ dollars.
worked_examples.context: the professor's example, and the reason he raises the two definitions: they differ by 13 cents here. The derivative is the standard meaning of marginal cost.

worked_examples.problem: Differentiate $y = \dfrac{x - 1}{x + 1}$ and say what the sign of the answer tells you.
worked_examples.answer: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{(1)(x+1) - (x-1)(1)}{(x+1)^{2}} = \dfrac{2}{(x+1)^{2}}$, which is positive wherever it is defined, so $y$ is increasing on each side of $x = -1$.
worked_examples.context: the professor's warm-up on this slide; a quotient rule revision with a rate reading

worked_examples.problem: A particle falls with $x(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^{2}$. Find its velocity and acceleration at time $t$.
worked_examples.context: constant acceleration; the velocity grows linearly with time

applied_contexts: particle motion in one dimension
marginal cost and marginal revenue
any quantity described as a 'rate' or 'per unit'
common_errors: Confusing speed with velocity — velocity carries a sign, speed does not
Reading a negative velocity as 'slowing down' rather than 'moving the other way'
Treating marginal cost as an average cost
Dropping the units, which is where the interpretation lives
Differentiating with respect to the wrong variable in a problem with more than one

topics.title: Marginal Analysis in Economics
topics.student_facing_name: Understanding marginal cost, revenue, and profit
topics.summary: Marginal cost, marginal revenue and marginal profit as derivatives, and what they mean to someone running a business. The marginal cost at an output level is very nearly the cost of the next unit, so comparing marginal revenue with marginal cost answers the question 'is one more unit worth making?'. This is the strand the professor teaches alongside the textbook rather than from it, and it recurs in the applications and integration units.
method_steps: Find $C'(x)$, $R'(x)$, and $P'(x)$ as the marginal functions
Evaluate the derivative at a specific production level $k$ to estimate the cost/revenue/profit of the next unit
Compare the marginal value to the actual incremental value $C(k+1) - C(k)$ to show how close the derivative approximation is

worked_examples.problem: A manufacturer estimates that when $x$ units of a commodity are produced, total cost will be $C(x) = \frac{1}{8}x^2 + 3x + 98$ dollars. (a) Find $C'(x)$ and compute $C'(8)$. (b) Find $C(9) - C(8)$. (c) Is $C'(8)$ close to $C(9) - C(8)$?
worked_examples.context: Demonstrates how marginal cost approximates actual incremental cost

worked_examples.problem: A manufacturer estimates that when $x$ units are produced, all units will be sold when price is $p(x) = \frac{1}{3}(75 - x)$ dollars per unit. (a) Find the marginal revenue function and use it to estimate revenue from selling the ninth unit. (b) What is the actual revenue from selling the ninth unit? (c) How close is marginal revenue to actual?
worked_examples.answer: $R(x) = p(x) \cdot x = \frac{1}{3}(75 - x) \cdot x$; compute $R'(x)$, then $R'(8)$ and $R(9) - R(8)$
worked_examples.context: Marginal revenue with price-dependent demand

worked_examples.problem: A manufacturer estimates $C(x) = \frac{1}{8}x^2 + 3x + 98$ and $p(x) = \frac{1}{3}(75 - x)$. (a) Find the marginal profit function and estimate profit from selling the ninth unit. (b) What is the actual profit? (c) Compare.
worked_examples.context: Marginal profit combines marginal revenue and marginal cost

applied_contexts: pricing and demand
production planning
unit cost analysis
incremental business decisions
common_errors: Confusing marginal (derivative) with total (function value)
Forgetting that marginal is an approximation and will not exactly equal the actual incremental change
Computing $C(k) - C(k+1)$ instead of $C(k+1) - C(k)$ (sign error)

topics.title: Critical Points
topics.student_facing_name: Finding the points where a curve might turn
topics.summary: A critical point of $f$ is a point $x = a$ in the domain where $f'(a) = 0$, or where $f'(a)$ does not exist. These are the only candidates for a local maximum or minimum, so every question about the largest or smallest value of a function starts here. Finding them is a two-step job: differentiate, then solve $f'(x) = 0$. The professor's worked cases are chosen so that the solving is the interesting part.
method_steps: Differentiate to get $f'(x)$
Set $f'(x) = 0$ and solve for $x$
Also note any point of the domain where $f'$ fails to exist
Check each solution actually lies in the domain of $f$
These are the critical points — they are candidates only, not yet classified

worked_examples.problem: Find the critical points of $y = x^{2} + 1$.
worked_examples.context: the simplest case, used to fix the procedure before the algebra gets harder

worked_examples.problem: Find the critical points of $y = x^{2}e^{-x}$.
worked_examples.answer: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2xe^{-x} + x^{2}(-1)e^{-x} = (2x - x^{2})e^{-x} = x(2-x)e^{-x}$, so the critical points are $x = 0$ and $x = 2$.
worked_examples.context: the professor's example. The key move is that $e^{-x} = \dfrac{1}{e^{x}}$ is never zero, so only the polynomial factor can vanish — he spends a whole slide on that point.
the cubic the professor carries through the whole first-derivative-test section; factor out the 6 before factorising

applied_contexts: the output level at which profit might be greatest
the dimensions at which a container might use least material
common_errors: Setting $f(x) = 0$ instead of $f'(x) = 0$
Concluding that a factor like $e^{-x}$ can be zero
Assuming every critical point is a maximum or a minimum — it may be neither
Losing a solution by dividing through by a factor containing $x$ instead of factorising
Forgetting points where the derivative does not exist
topics.geogebra_prompt: Plot $f(x) = 2x^3 + 3x^2 - 12x - 7$ with $f'(x)$ underneath, marking where the lower graph crosses the axis and what the upper graph does there

topics.title: Extreme Values on a Closed Interval
topics.student_facing_name: The largest and smallest values a function reaches
topics.summary: The professor states the guarantee plainly: every continuous function on a closed interval attains both a smallest value and a largest value on that interval. These are the absolute, or global, extrema. They occur either at a critical point inside the interval or at one of the two endpoints, so the search is finite — evaluate $f$ at every critical point and at both endpoints, and compare. He stresses that the answer depends on the domain: change the interval and the extrema can change with it.
method_steps: Check the function is continuous on the closed interval
Find all critical points and keep only those inside the interval
Evaluate $f$ at each of those critical points
Evaluate $f$ at both endpoints $a$ and $b$
The largest of these values is the absolute maximum, the smallest the absolute minimum

worked_examples.problem: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of $g(x) = x^{2/3}$ on $[-2, 3]$.
worked_examples.answer: $g'(x) = \tfrac{2}{3}x^{-1/3}$, which does not exist at $x = 0$, so $x = 0$ is a critical point. Comparing $g(0) = 0$, $g(-2) = 2^{2/3} \approx 1.587$ and $g(3) = 3^{2/3} \approx 2.08$: the minimum is $0$ at $x = 0$ and the maximum is $3^{2/3}$ at $x = 3$.
worked_examples.context: the professor opens the integration lecture with this same function. It is chosen because the critical point comes from the derivative failing to exist, not from it being zero.

worked_examples.problem: Find the extreme values of $f(x) = x^{2} + 1$ on $[-1, 2]$.
worked_examples.answer: The only critical point is $x = 0$, with $f(0) = 1$. The endpoints give $f(-1) = 2$ and $f(2) = 5$. So the minimum is $1$ at $x = 0$ and the maximum is $5$ at $x = 2$.
worked_examples.context: the maximum is at an endpoint, not a critical point — which is exactly why endpoints have to be tested

applied_contexts: the best output level when production capacity is limited
the highest and lowest temperature over a fixed period
common_errors: Forgetting to test the endpoints
Including critical points that fall outside the interval
Reporting the $x$ value where the maximum occurs as the maximum value itself
Applying the guarantee to an open interval or to a function with a break in it
Assuming the absolute maximum must be at a critical point
topics.geogebra_prompt: Plot a function with draggable interval endpoints and highlight the highest and lowest points of the visible piece, so the extrema visibly jump between critical points and endpoints

topics.title: Monotonic Functions: Intervals of Increase and Decrease
topics.student_facing_name: Using the sign of the derivative to say where a curve rises and falls
topics.summary: The sign of $f'$ decides the direction of $f$: where $f'(x) > 0$ the function is increasing, and where $f'(x) < 0$ it is decreasing. Since $f'$ can only change sign at a critical point, the critical points cut the domain into intervals on which the direction is constant. Testing one convenient value of $f'$ in each interval therefore settles the behaviour on the whole interval — the professor's phrase is to pick a point $c$ with $a < c < b$ and look at the sign of $f'(c)$.
method_steps: Find the critical points
Use them to split the domain into open intervals
Choose one test value $c$ inside each interval
Evaluate $f'(c)$ and record only its sign
Report: increasing where the sign is positive, decreasing where it is negative

worked_examples.problem: For $f(x) = 2x^{3} + 3x^{2} - 12x - 7$, find the intervals on which $f$ is increasing and decreasing.
worked_examples.answer: Critical points $x = -2$ and $x = 1$ split the line into $(-\infty, -2)$, $(-2, 1)$ and $(1, \infty)$. Testing $c = -3$: $f'(-3) = 54 - 18 - 12 = 32 > 0$. Testing $c = 0$: $f'(0) = -12 < 0$. Testing $c = 2$: $f'(2) = 24 + 12 - 12 = 24 > 0$. So $f$ increases on $(-\infty, -2)$, decreases on $(-2, 1)$, and increases on $(1, \infty)$.
worked_examples.context: the professor's fully worked case, spread across three slides. Note he evaluates $f'$ at the test point, not $f$, and only the sign is used.

worked_examples.problem: For $f(x) = x^{2} + 1$, where is $f$ increasing and where decreasing?
worked_examples.answer: $f'(x) = 2x$, critical point $x = 0$. At $c = -1$, $f'(-1) = -2 < 0$; at $c = 1$, $f'(1) = 2 > 0$. So $f$ decreases on $(-\infty, 0)$ and increases on $(0, \infty)$.
worked_examples.context: the parabola, done the same way so the method is seen on a graph students already know

applied_contexts: trend analysis
business metrics
production efficiency over time
common_errors: Testing the critical point itself instead of a point strictly inside an interval
Substituting the test value into $f$ rather than $f'$
Computing the whole value of $f'(c)$ carefully when only its sign is needed — harmless, but slow
Writing the intervals as closed rather than open
Assuming the sign must alternate between consecutive intervals
topics.geogebra_prompt: f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5; plot f(x), f'(x); mark critical points and shade increasing/decreasing regions

topics.title: The First Derivative Test
topics.student_facing_name: Deciding whether a critical point is a peak or a trough
topics.summary: Once the sign of $f'$ is known either side of a critical point, the nature of that point follows. If $f'$ changes from positive to negative there, the function rises then falls, so the point is a local maximum. If $f'$ changes from negative to positive, it is a local minimum. If the sign does not change, the point is neither. The professor defines a relative maximum as a point whose value is larger than the values at nearby points — a local claim, not a claim about the whole graph.
method_steps: Find the critical points
Build the sign chart of $f'$ on the intervals between them
At each critical point, read the sign to its left and to its right
Positive then negative means a local maximum; negative then positive means a local minimum
Substitute back into $f$ to get the value at that maximum or minimum

worked_examples.answer: $f'$ is positive on $(-\infty, -2)$, negative on $(-2, 1)$ and positive on $(1, \infty)$. So $x = -2$ is a local maximum and $x = 1$ is a local minimum.
worked_examples.context: the professor's main worked example, continued from the sign chart. $f(-2) = 13$ and $f(1) = -14$.

worked_examples.problem: Classify the critical point of $f(x) = x^{2} + 1$.
worked_examples.answer: $f'$ is negative on $(-\infty, 0)$ and positive on $(0, \infty)$, so $x = 0$ is a local minimum, with value $f(0) = 1$.
worked_examples.context: the sign goes from negative to positive, which is the minimum pattern

applied_contexts: the output level that maximises profit
the moment a quantity stops growing and starts shrinking
common_errors: Getting the two patterns the wrong way round — rising then falling is a maximum
Concluding a critical point must be one or the other when the sign does not change at all
Confusing a local maximum with the absolute maximum on an interval
Reporting the critical $x$ value as the maximum instead of $f$ at that value
topics.geogebra_prompt: A tangent line sliding along a cubic, with the sign of its slope shown, so the changeover from positive to negative can be seen happening at the peak

topics.title: Second-Derivative Test for Maxima and Minima
topics.student_facing_name: Using the second derivative to find max and min
topics.summary: A quicker alternative to the sign chart when the second derivative is easy to compute. At a critical point where $f'(a) = 0$: if $f''(a) < 0$ the point is a local maximum, if $f''(a) > 0$ it is a local minimum, and if $f''(a) = 0$ the test says nothing and the first derivative test has to be used instead. The professor presents it as the second of two tools for the same job, not as a replacement for the first.
method_steps: Find $f'(x)$ and set it equal to zero
Solve for critical points (stationary values)
Find $f''(x)$
Evaluate $f''$ at each critical point
If $f''< 0$ at that point, it is a maximum; if $f'' > 0$, it is a minimum
(Optional) Calculate the actual maximum or minimum value by substituting back into $f(x)$

worked_examples.problem: Investigate the maxima and minima of $y = 2x^3 + 3x^2 - 36x + 10$
worked_examples.context: Pure optimization problem

worked_examples.problem: Investigate the maxima and minima of $y = 2x^3 + 9x^2 - 60x + 5$
worked_examples.context: Pure optimization problem

worked_examples.problem: Investigate the maxima and minima of $y = 2x^3 - 21x^2 + 60x - 8$
worked_examples.context: Pure optimization problem

applied_contexts: economics
business
manufacturing
common_errors: Applying the test at a point that is not a critical point
Reading $f''(a) < 0$ as a minimum — negative means the curve bends downwards, so it is a maximum
Treating $f''(a) = 0$ as proof that the point is neither, when the test is simply silent
Differentiating only once and testing the sign of $f'$ at the point, which is zero by construction

topics.title: Applied Optimization
topics.student_facing_name: Turning a word problem into a maximum or minimum
topics.summary: The hard part of an optimization problem is never the calculus — it is getting from the words to a single function of a single variable. The professor gives a five-step procedure for this and then applies the three tools already available (extreme values on a closed interval, the first derivative test, the second derivative test) to the function that results. The examples are geometric: the largest rectangle inside a semicircle, and the one-litre can using the least metal.
notation: domain of the variable being optimized
method_steps: Read the problem carefully: what is given, and what quantity is to be optimized?
Draw a picture and label it with everything known
Introduce variables and write every relation in the problem as an equation
Write an equation for the quantity to be optimized, using the constraint to reduce it to one variable
Find the critical points, then test them and the endpoints of the domain, and classify

worked_examples.problem: A rectangle is to be inscribed in a semicircle of radius 2, with its base on the diameter. What is the largest area it can have, and what are its dimensions?
worked_examples.answer: Put the semicircle as $y = \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}$ with the rectangle running from $-x$ to $x$. Area $A(x) = 2x\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}$ on $[0, 2]$. Setting $A'(x) = 0$ gives $x = \sqrt{2}$, so the rectangle is $2\sqrt{2}$ wide and $\sqrt{2}$ tall, with area $4$.
worked_examples.context: the professor's worked example. The constraint is the equation of the circle; it is what turns two variables into one.

worked_examples.problem: Design a one-litre can shaped like a right circular cylinder. What dimensions use the least material?
worked_examples.answer: With volume fixed at $1000\ \text{cm}^3 = \pi r^{2}h$, the surface area is $A(r) = 2\pi r^{2} + 2\pi r h = 2\pi r^{2} + \dfrac{2000}{r}$. Setting $A'(r) = 4\pi r - \dfrac{2000}{r^{2}} = 0$ gives $r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{500}{\pi}} \approx 5.42$ cm, and then $h \approx 10.84$ cm — the height is twice the radius.
worked_examples.context: the professor's second example. The volume constraint eliminates $h$; the answer $h = 2r$ is worth remembering as a sanity check.

applied_contexts: least material for a container of fixed volume
largest enclosed area for a fixed length of fencing
cheapest production schedule subject to a requirement
common_errors: Differentiating a function of two variables without using the constraint to eliminate one
Optimizing the wrong quantity — maximising the perimeter when the area was asked for
Ignoring the natural domain, so a negative length or radius survives as an 'answer'
Stopping at the critical value of $x$ without answering the question that was asked
Forgetting to check the endpoints of the domain
